issues.legal_issue: The statutory duty to supply electricity is subject to applicable charges, requirements, and reasonable conditions prescribed by the electricity utilities.
The duty to supply electricity under the governing statute is owed to the owner or occupier seeking supply, rather than to the premises independently of its owner or occupier.
An application by a new owner or occupier for electricity supply is a fresh connection, while an application by the same consumer for the same premises after disconnection is a reconnection.
Statutory conditions of supply made under the former electricity legislation may require a new owner or occupier to clear the previous consumer’s arrears before receiving electricity supply.
The regulatory powers under the current electricity legislation permit State Commissions to prescribe conditions for recovering a previous consumer’s arrears from a subsequent owner or occupier.

Subordinate legislation under the current electricity legislation may create a statutory charge for electricity arrears on premises and provide for recovery from a transferee, subject to applicable notice requirements.

Electricity arrears do not automatically constitute a charge on premises, and a transferee is not liable for a previous consumer’s arrears in the absence of an applicable statutory condition or express statutory charge.
The two-year limitation in the electricity statute restricts disconnection as a recovery remedy but does not extinguish the utility’s right to pursue civil or other lawful recovery remedies.
A sale on an “as is where is” basis may put an auction purchaser on notice of liabilities affecting the property, including electricity dues, depending on the sale terms and circumstances.

A rehabilitation scheme under the sick-industries legislation may override inconsistent electricity-supply conditions where the scheme governs the parties and allocates responsibility for the arrears.
